scope: Successor forensic pass over the historical Project-Frankenstein approval path requested by the current Triggerword-5 frontier. Source-only; no runtime promotion.

atoms.what_it_does: request_approval() creates an 8-character UUID-derived approval_id and stores tool_name/tool_input/risk/reason/timestamp under that id. wait_for_approval() checks responses by approval_id. However ToolExecutor.execute() accepts only tool_name, tool_input and skip_approval; after approval, AgentLoop calls execute(..., skip_approval=True) without passing approval_id or a request digest into the execution boundary.
atoms.why_it_exists: The historical overlay needed a simple human approval handshake before risky tool execution.
dependencies: AgentLoop preserves the same tool_call variables across request and later execute call by convention
atoms.failure_mode: Approval is not mechanically bound at execute() to the exact approved input, generation or invocation identity. A trusted caller is expected to preserve the same tool/input; skip_approval=True is itself a caller-controlled bypass. Therefore approval_id is useful lineage but not a sufficient Frankenstein-2.0 effect token.
atoms.concurrency_implication: Different approvals are keyed independently, but the execution boundary does not consume or invalidate the approval id; exact once-only invocation binding is absent from the inspected path.
atoms.privacy_implication: The approval queue persists full tool_input in JSON; this is a historical privacy surface that should not be copied directly into a canonical effect journal.
atoms.latency_or_cost_implication: Polling waits up to 120 seconds in AgentLoop for risky calls.
atoms.state_lifetime: approval files plus in-memory request map; no execution-bound token lifetime
known_counterevidence: The inspected AgentLoop does pass the same in-memory tool_call.action/tool_call.action_input after approval, reducing accidental mismatch in that caller. This is source-level caller discipline, not an invariant enforced by ToolExecutor.execute().
open_questions: Whether any historical overlay or executor wrapper independently verified the approved request contents immediately before execution.
Whether approval responses were one-shot consumed or could remain reusable in historical runtime state.

atoms.what_it_does: AgentLoop auto-approves a fixed tool-name set and otherwise requests approval. Both the safe path and the approved risky path invoke ToolExecutor.execute(..., skip_approval=True), so the final executor relies on caller classification/approval discipline rather than independently consuming a typed approval decision.
atoms.why_it_exists: Keep read-only/low-risk actions fast while preserving human approval for mutating tools.
outputs: execute with skip_approval=True or denied ToolResult
atoms.failure_mode: Tool-name safety can drift from argument-level semantics, and caller-controlled skip_approval means the executor does not independently prove that the current invocation was the approved one.
atoms.concurrency_implication: A future typed gate must bind approval/decision to immutable invocation identity and request digest, not only tool name or session context.
known_counterevidence: Historical source does implement real pre-execution denial in the ordinary AgentLoop path when user approval is not granted; the defect here is exact decision-to-execution binding, not absence of any enforcement.
open_questions: Recover production reachability of this historical AgentLoop before granting runtime lineage credit.

hypotheses: The historical AgentLoop/ToolExecutor supplies a useful conceptual predecessor for true pre-execution enforcement, but its approval identity should be treated as UI/workflow correlation rather than a canonical effect capability because execute() does not consume the approval id or approved request digest.

Frankenstein 2.0 should combine historical pre-execution deny behavior with the newer post-execution journal, while binding EffectDecision to immutable invocation_id/tool_use_id + request_digest + generation and consuming that decision at the actual executor boundary.
counterhypotheses: A historical wrapper outside these files may have revalidated tool input against the approval request before execute(); no such binding is established by the inspected source.
If the historical runtime was strictly single-threaded and AgentLoop was the only caller, caller discipline may have made mismatches rare; that does not make it a reusable authority contract.
contradictions: Historical Project-Frankenstein has real pre-execution human denial, but the approval decision is not structurally consumed by the executor invocation; both facts must be preserved.

The later stern.py path adds richer generation/idempotency/outcome bookkeeping but intentionally does not generically block execution; the two lineages each contain a missing half of the desired Frankenstein-2.0 EffectGate/EffectJournal contract.
critical_unknowns: Production reachability of AgentLoop/ToolExecutor at the pinned historical commit.
Whether external overlay code one-shot consumed approvals or revalidated request contents before execution.
Exact source/runtime lineage of wache-koenig.py between historical AgentLoop enforcement and current stern.py bookkeeping.
Exact installed hook scheduler behavior for parallel current-donor tool calls.
